result:
If you give me a thousand words, the first thing I notice is not the words at all, but the space they are supposed to fill. A thousand is a generous number. It is large enough to wander in, to get a little lost, and small enough that you can feel the edges if you stand still for a moment and listen. It is not empty, exactly. It is open. Like a room in the afternoon with the windows left open, the curtains moving a little, the light coming in sideways and making everything look more honest than it usually does. I could spend all thousand words just describing that feeling of being given permission to begin without a purpose. That might even be the point.

So I begin, naturally, with morning. Not a dramatic morning, not a sunrise over a mountain, just a regular morning in a kitchen where the kettle is making that low, promising sound before it boils. I make tea or coffee, whichever is closer, and I stand by the window while I wait and watch the street do its ordinary work. A neighbor walking a dog that is much smaller than its coat. A bus sighing at the stop. Someone laughing, far away, for a reason I will never know. There is a comfort in these small, unimportant things that I did not understand when I was younger and always wanted something bigger to happen. Bigger rarely arrives. Smaller arrives every day, quietly, and asks to be noticed.

I think about memory now, because morning does that to a person. Memory is not a library, despite what we like to say. It is not organized. It is more like a house you lived in for a long time, where you remember the kitchen clearly and the hallway only as a feeling, where some rooms are locked not because you locked them but because you simply never go there anymore. I remember the way my grandmother folded laundry on the bed, quickly, with her hands doing the work before her mind had to be involved. I remember a bicycle with a bent wheel that made a soft clicking sound every rotation. I do not remember what I was worried about last Tuesday, and that feels like a mercy. Perhaps forgetting is not a failure of memory. Perhaps it is memory being kind, editing the manuscript to leave only the parts that matter.

Words themselves are strange tools. We use them to connect, and they fail us constantly, and we keep using them anyway because there is nothing better. I have tried, at different points in my life, to believe that if I just found the perfect sentence, the perfect combination, it would say everything I wanted to say about love or grief or joy and people would finally understand. That was a young person's hope. Now I think a sentence is more like a hand extended. It does not contain the whole person. It just reaches. Sometimes it is taken. Sometimes it waves in the air for a while. But still, we extend it again. We write the message, we send the text, we say the thing we are a little afraid to say, and we hope that the reaching is enough.

Outside, the weather is changing. It has been changing all my life, and I have only recently started paying attention to it in the right way. Not as a forecast, not as a problem to plan around, but as a companion. Rain on a window is a sound I could listen to forever. Wind in the trees behind the house has its own language, low and continuous, like someone telling a story over and over without ever finishing. I spent years indoors, mostly, with headphones on, convinced that the important music was coming from somewhere else. The trees were having their own concert the whole time, for free, without any intermission. I am trying, late, to learn how to listen to the world that does not need me to listen to it. It seems generous that it continues anyway.

People are the hardest and best part of all of this. I have known people who could make a room feel larger just by entering it, not by being loud, but by being truly there. I have known people who were lonely in a crowd. I have been both of those people, on different days. Conversation, real conversation, is a rare and fragile thing. Most talking is just trading information, reporting weather, exchanging schedules. But sometimes, someone asks a question and actually waits for the answer, and suddenly you are both somewhere else entirely, telling the truth because it feels safer than lying. I try to be that kind of listener now. I do not always succeed. I interrupt. I think of my own story while someone else is telling theirs. But I am learning to stay.

Music helps when words give up. I have a song that I associate with a particular summer, and another with a particular heartbreak, and another that I play when I have to clean the apartment and pretend I am in a film. The songs do not explain anything. They just hold a feeling in a shape that fits in the ear. A melody can carry a person across a room full of years without them having to say a word. I wish more of my life had that quality, that a few notes could sum it up and let everyone in on the secret. Maybe it does, and I am just not listening to myself the way I listen to songs. Maybe my walk to the store, my way of making tea, my habit of humming without noticing, are also a kind of music.

There is work, of course. There is always work. Some of it is meaningful, some of it is just necessary, and most of it is a mixture that changes from day to day. I used to think that if I found the right work, everything else would fall into place, as if work were a key to a locked door. Now I think work is more like weather too. It comes, it goes, it rains, it clears. On good days, I can lose myself in it and time passes in a way that feels almost physical, warm on the skin. On bad days, I count the minutes and wonder what I am doing with my life. Both kinds of days are teaching me something, though the bad days are slower teachers and I would prefer not to take their class again.

Time is the strangest thing I have encountered. When I was a child, a summer felt like a country I could move into. Now summers arrive and leave like polite guests. I do not know when this changed, or if it changed in me or in the world. Perhaps both. Perhaps time speeds up because there is more of it behind you, so each new year is a smaller portion of the whole. That makes sense mathematically, but it does not make it feel any less strange. I am older than I think I am, most mornings. Then a song comes on, or someone laughs in a way that reminds me of someone I knew, and I am briefly, completely, the age I was then. We are all many ages at once, stacked like plates. It is a wonder we do not break more often.

I walk past a tree on my way to the store that has been there longer than the street. I do not know its name. I could look it up. I could learn its species and its history and its favorite kind of soil, and that knowledge would be nice, but mostly I just like that it is there. It does not ask for my attention. It offers shade in summer and a kind of architecture in winter, bare branches against the sky like a drawing someone made from memory. Cities are full of these quiet residents. We pave around them and build our lives in their margins and pretend we are in charge. Every spring they prove, gently, that they were here first and they will be here after the buildings have been replaced by other buildings.

I think about endings, not in a morbid way, but in the way you think about the last page of a book you have enjoyed. Knowing it ends is part of why it matters. If this conversation, this day, this life, went on forever, I suspect I would stop paying attention. Forever is too long for attention. A thousand words is about right for attention, I think. Long enough to say something true, short enough to mean it. I have lost people. I have lost versions of myself. Each loss has left a shape in me, like a chair where someone used to sit, and I have learned to live around those shapes without pretending they are not there. Grief is not a problem to be solved. It is a room you learn to live in, with the windows eventually open again.

The future, from where I sit, is both exciting and a little lonely. I write these words knowing that machines can write now, can mimic, can produce a thousand words in seconds without ever having made tea in the morning or watched a tree. That does not frighten me as much as I thought it would. It clarifies something. The words are not the point. The having lived is the point. A machine can arrange words. It cannot remember a bent bicycle wheel. It cannot be grateful for rain. It cannot sit by a window and feel its own small life being part of something larger. I am not against the future. I am, in fact, curious about it. I just want to remember, while it arrives, what it felt like to be human and slow and a little unsure, and to write anyway.

So here I am, near the end of my thousand, and I find I do not have anything profound to conclude with. I have some mornings, some trees, some people I love, some songs I cannot explain. That seems like enough material for a life, let alone a thousand words. If I had a thousand more, I would probably talk about the grocery list, and the book I keep meaning to finish, and the dream I had last night where I was looking for a room in a house I used to live in. I would talk about how ordinary everything is, and how that ordinariness, looked at closely, is not ordinary at all. For now, I will stop here, with the kettle still warm, the window still open, and the day still, mercifully, unfinished.
